\chapter{How You Get There}
\label{ch:el-coche-y-el-avion}
\hlchaptermodality{363}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el coche, el avión, el barco, el autobús and la bicicleta, and say which one I am taking.}

Complete ES-C363-bicicleta: name five ways to reach a place, and say which one you are taking.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el coche]{el coche — the car named after a Hungarian village}

\label{lesson:ES-C363-coche}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the fire}, then \emph{the moon}. (\emph{El fuego}; \emph{la luna}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el camino — the thing a coche needs underneath it.
  \item el viaje — what you take a coche on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KO-che}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ch} is the sound English has in \emph{church}, and the opening \emph{c} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el coche} — \textquotedblleft{}the car.\textquotedblright{}

A village did this. \textbf{Kocs} is a small place west of Budapest, and in the fifteenth century its wagon-makers worked out how to hang a carriage body on straps, so that the passengers stopped being shaken to pieces on a long road. Hungarian called the result a \textbf{kocsi szekér}, a \textquotedblleft{}cart from Kocs\textquotedblright{}, then dropped the \emph{szekér} and kept \textbf{kocsi}, \textquotedblleft{}the Kocs one\textquotedblright{}. It is attested in that sense from 1469.

Europe wanted the ride, and took the name with it. German made \textbf{Kutsche} of it, French made \textbf{coche}, and Spanish took \emph{coche} from French. English took it too and spelled it \textbf{coach} by the 1550s. So \emph{coche} and \emph{coach} are one word in two spellings, and underneath both of them there is still a village.

Then English did something odd with it. At Oxford and Cambridge, a tutor who carried a struggling student through an examination was called a \textbf{coach} — student slang, the tutor as vehicle. Sport borrowed the joke, and now a coach shouts from the touchline with no memory at all of the wagon-makers.

One warning, and it matters the moment you travel: \emph{coche} is the car in \textbf{Spain}. Across much of Latin America the car is \emph{carro} or \emph{auto} instead, and in some countries \emph{coche} means a pram, or is a word nobody reaches for.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the thing in the driveway, and you know why a stagecoach and a football coach share a word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el coche}
  \item \emph{el coche nuevo}
  \item \emph{un coche en el camino}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is Kocs? (A town west of Budapest whose sprung carriages were famous.) And which English word is \emph{coche}? (Coach.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el avión]{el avión — a bird-word that was coined, not inherited}

\label{lesson:ES-C363-avion}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the moon}, then \emph{the car}. (\emph{La luna}; \emph{el coche}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el cielo — where an avión spends its time.
  \item el viaje — what you board one for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-BYON}, two beats with the weight on the second, which is what the written accent is telling you. The \emph{v} is the same sound as a Spanish \emph{b}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el avión} — \textquotedblleft{}the aeroplane.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{avis} was a bird, and it is all over the learned end of English: \textbf{aviation}, an \textbf{aviator}, an \textbf{aviary}, anything \textbf{avian}. It hides inside two bird names worn smooth by use — an \textbf{ostrich} is \emph{avis struthio}, a \textquotedblleft{}sparrow-bird\textquotedblright{}, and a \textbf{bustard} is \emph{avis tarda}, a \textquotedblleft{}slow bird\textquotedblright{}. And under \textbf{auspices} there is a Roman standing in a field reading the flight of birds for omens: \emph{avis} plus \emph{specere}, to watch.

Here is the part that matters about \emph{avión}, though. Spanish did not inherit it. \emph{Avis} dropped out of everyday Latin as it became Spanish, and stayed out. The word you are learning was manufactured in French, in 1875, by \textbf{Clément Ader}, who built \emph{avis} into a name for a flying machine before anyone had flown one. Spanish borrowed the finished French word, accent and all. It is a nineteenth-century invention in a Roman costume.

Which springs a trap that was set for you long ago. \textbf{El aviso}, the notice, belongs to a different family entirely. It comes through French \emph{aviser}, from Latin \emph{vidēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} — the root of \textbf{vision}, \textbf{video}, \textbf{advise} and \textbf{evident}, and by inheritance of \textbf{wit}, \textbf{wise} and \textbf{witness}. One is a bird-root, the other a see-root. Four letters apart, no relation.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name what crosses the sky, and you can hold \emph{el avión} and \emph{el aviso} apart by their roots.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el avión}
  \item \emph{el avión en el cielo}
  \item \emph{un viaje en avión}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Who made the word \emph{avión}, and when? (Clément Ader, in French, in 1875.) And does \emph{el aviso} come from the same root? (No — it is from \emph{vidēre}, to see.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el barco]{el barco — the little boat that grew}

\label{lesson:ES-C363-barco}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the car}, then \emph{the aeroplane}. (\emph{El coche}; \emph{el avión}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el mar — what a barco crosses.
  \item el puerto — where it stops.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BAR-ko}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} is one quick tap of the tongue, not a roll. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el barco} — \textquotedblleft{}the ship.\textquotedblright{}

Late Latin \textbf{barca} was a small boat, the kind you rowed. It turns up in writing around 400 AD, and where it came from before that is unsettled. The usual suggestion runs back through Greek \emph{baris}, a flat-bottomed Egyptian river boat — plausible, often repeated, and never actually demonstrated. Careful sources hedge it, and so should you. Take \emph{barca} as the oldest firm ground.

Forward from there the trail is clean. Old French made \textbf{barge} of it. Italian \emph{barca} came into French as \emph{barque}, and English took that as \textbf{bark}, the sailing ship of every poem about the sea. To \textbf{embark} is to be put into a \emph{barque}; to \textbf{disembark} is to climb back out. Board a plane tomorrow and you are still, in Latin, being loaded into a small rowing boat.

English then hands you a three-way trap. The \textbf{bark} that is a ship is this Romance word. The \textbf{bark} on a tree is Old Norse, \emph{borkr}. The \textbf{bark} of a dog is Old English, \emph{beorcan}. Three words spelled alike, related to nothing.

And Spanish kept a distinction of size that English lost along the way: \emph{barca} stayed the little rowing boat it had been, while \emph{barco} grew up into the ship in general. The word you are learning is the small one that got big.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name a ship, and you know that to embark is to be lowered into a rowing boat.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el barco}
  \item \emph{el barco en el mar}
  \item \emph{un barco en el puerto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{barca} mean in Late Latin? (A small boat.) And are the three English barks one word? (No — a ship, a tree and a dog, three separate origins.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el autobús]{el autobús — two words, each cut in half}

\label{lesson:ES-C363-autobus}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the aeroplane}, then \emph{the ship}. (\emph{El avión}; \emph{el barco}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el asiento — what you hope to find on one.
  \item la parada — where it picks you up.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{au-to-BUS}, three beats with the weight on the last, which is why the \emph{u} carries a written accent. The opening \emph{au} is one glide, not two beats. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el autobús} — \textquotedblleft{}the bus.\textquotedblright{}

Take the back half first, because it may be the strangest word in this book. Latin \textbf{omnis} meant \textquotedblleft{}all\textquotedblright{}. Latin hung its grammar on the ends of words, and \textbf{omnibus} is one of those endings at work: the dative plural, \textquotedblleft{}for all, to everybody\textquotedblright{}. It is not a noun. It is \emph{omnis} wearing a grammatical hat.

Around 1823, in Nantes, a carriage service began running from a spot outside the shop of a hatter named \textbf{Omnès}. His sign read \textbf{Omnes Omnibus} — \textquotedblleft{}Omnès for everybody\textquotedblright{}, a pun on his own name. Passengers took the joke for the name of the vehicle, and \emph{omnibus} became the French word for a public carriage. English borrowed it whole.

Then French tired of the length and cut it short — and cut in an astonishing place. It kept \emph{-bus} and threw away \emph{omn-}, the entire stem, the part carrying the meaning. So the \textbf{bus} of English, Spanish and French is a Latin case ending, orphaned from its word, walking around doing a noun's work.

The front half is a second clipping. \emph{Auto-} is chopped off \textbf{automóvil}, which was itself assembled as a hybrid: Greek \emph{autós}, \textquotedblleft{}self\textquotedblright{}, bolted onto Latin \emph{mōbilis}, \textquotedblleft{}movable\textquotedblright{}. Two clippings, three languages, one vehicle.

It is also the most regional word in this chain. \emph{Autobús} is what Spain says; Mexico says \emph{camión}, the Caribbean and the Canaries \emph{guagua}, Argentina \emph{colectivo}, Chile \emph{micro}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the thing at the stop, and you know that \emph{bus} is a Latin ending with its own word cut away.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el autobús}
  \item \emph{el asiento del autobús}
  \item \emph{la parada del autobús}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which part of Latin \emph{omnis} is \emph{-bus}? (The dative plural ending, meaning for all.) And who was Omnès? (A hatter in Nantes whose punning sign named the vehicle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la bicicleta]{la bicicleta — two Greek wheels on a Latin prefix}

\label{lesson:ES-C363-bicicleta}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the ship}, then \emph{the bus}. (\emph{El barco}; \emph{el autobús}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la calle — where you ride one.
  \item el parque — where you ride one without traffic.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bi-si-KLE-ta}, four beats with the weight on the third. The first \emph{c} softens in front of the \emph{i}; the second stays hard in front of the \emph{l}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la bicicleta} — \textquotedblleft{}the bicycle.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{kyklos} was a circle, and also a wheel — one idea looked at twice. Latin \textbf{bi-} is \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}. French set them together as \textbf{bicyclette} in the nineteenth century, and Spanish took the French word entire. Like a good many machines of that decade, it is a hybrid: a Latin prefix bolted onto a Greek noun by people who needed a name in a hurry.

\emph{Kyklos} has been generous. A \textbf{cycle} turns and comes back to where it began. A \textbf{tricycle} has three wheels; a \textbf{motorcycle} has an engine. A \textbf{cyclops} is a \textquotedblleft{}round-eye\textquotedblright{}. And a \textbf{cyclone} was minted in 1848 by Henry Piddington, who wanted a word for a storm that turns.

Now the part worth carrying away. English \textbf{wheel} is not borrowed from \emph{kyklos} at all — it is its \textbf{cousin}, come down the Germanic line from the same ancient root for turning. One of them arrived by ship; the other was never away. Both sit in the sentence \textquotedblleft{}I rode my bicycle\textquotedblright{}, and only one of them travelled.

One last thing, because it is a good story. \textbf{Encyclopedia} has no Greek original. Someone in the Renaissance read the two-word phrase \emph{enkyklios paideia}, \textquotedblleft{}a well-rounded education\textquotedblright{}, ran the halves together, and invented an ancestor for it.

A caution to finish: a \textbf{circus} and its ring are from Greek \emph{kirkos}, a different root. That is a family resemblance, not a family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the two-wheeled one, and you can tell a borrowed cousin from an inherited one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la bicicleta}
  \item \emph{la bicicleta en el parque}
  \item \emph{una bicicleta en la calle}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is English \emph{wheel} borrowed from \emph{kyklos}? (No — it is the inherited cousin.) And was \emph{encyclopedia} ever a Greek word? (No — it is a misreading of a two-word Greek phrase.)
\end{tcolorbox}
